text: The assembly will hear an address by His
Excellency Andras Varga Koranyi,
President of Hungary. I request protocol
to escort His Excellency and invite him
to address the assembly.
>> Mr. President,
Mr. Secretary-General,
excellencies,
it is a special honor to address this
assembly on behalf of Hungary.
I speak here to the nations of the
world,
but also to my fellow citizens watching
at home.
For much of my life, I served as a judge
in Hungary and at the European Court of
Human Rights.
That work taught me a simple lesson.
The law must apply even to those in
power.
This belief will guide me as president.
I will protect the Constitution, the
freedom of our institutions,
and the dignity of every Hungarian
citizen.
The state belongs to those who support
the government,
to those who oppose it,
and to those who have lost trust in
politics whatsoever.
A new political majority must not become
the new owner of the state.
This April,
the people of Hungary voted for
democratic renewal.
They expected more than a change of
government.
They expect public life to change,
rule of law,
a state that serves rather than
controls,
courts that decide without pressure,
a press that challenges power,
and public money that is used for public
goods.
There must be accountability for
corruption and abuse of power,
but there must be no revenge.
Justice cannot become a political
weapon.
A democratic state cannot repair past
wrongs by repeating them with new people
in charge.
The same law must apply to those who
governed yesterday,
those who govern today, and those who
may govern tomorrow.
A republic begins when power accepts its
limits.
That is the republic Hungary must now
rebuild.
Trust from our partners will not return
because of one election or one speech.
Hungary asked to be judged by what we
do.
We will be reliable member of the
European Union,
a committed NATO ally, and an active
member of the United United Nations.
These partnership do not take away our
freedom. They protect it.
Hungary will defend its national
interest,
but it will do
so as a partner.
We believe that national interest and
international cooperation do not have to
stand against each other.
For Hungarians, the reasons are part of
our
our own history.
70 years ago,
the revolution of 1956 expressed our
people's determination to govern
themselves.
Soviet tanks tanks crushed that hope.
Our appeals reached the United Nations,
but the international community could
not prevent our defeat.
Many countries represented here opened
their doors to Hungarians
who fled their country after the
revolution.
We remember both the cost of losing our
independence
and that help and and the help that
allowed our people to start again.
Today
Ukraine is fighting to preserve its
independence.
Hungary condemns Russia's full-scale war
of aggression as a violation of United
Nations Charter and international law.
We affirm Ukraine's right to
self-defense,
its sovereignty, and territorial
integrity within its internationally
recognized borders,
and the right of its people to decide
their own future.
The freedom Hungarians demanded for
themselves in 1956
is a freedom we must hold must uphold
for Ukrainians today.
We remember those who have lost their
lives in in this war, and we want
diplomacy to bring the killing to an
end.
But a lasting peace must respect
Ukraine's sovereignty.
If taking territory by force
becomes an accepted way of settling
disputes,
every smaller country will have reasons
to worry about its own future.
The principles of the charter therefore
therefore matter to all of us.
Human suffering cannot wait for
diplomacy to succeed.
People in conflict need food, medicine,
and protection now.
Hungary will continue to provide
humanitarian aid to people in danger,
especially the most vulnerable.
In the Middle East, we call for full
respect for international humanitarian
law and for aid to reach those who need
it safely and without interruption.
Israelis and Palesti- Palestinians must
be able to live in security and dignity.
A lasting peace must give their families
reasons to believe that their children
can grow up without the fear
that has marked so many lives.
For people forced from their homes by
war and or persecution,
protection may first mean finding safety
in another country.
Hungary's own history gives us reason to
understand that need.
At the same time, every state has the
right to protect its borders. Hungary
will do do so in accordance with
international law. We will fight illegal
migration
and the criminal networks that profit
from it while respecting human dignity
and the protection given to refugees.
But security is not only about borders
and war.
People also need a chance to build a
future where they live.
They need homes, schools, health care,
and ways to earn a living.
Poverty and the lack of opportunity can
drive people from their countries just
as conflicts can.
Hungary will continue to support
development that helps communities build
that future
based on their own needs and priorities.
We are ready to share our our
in education, health, and digital
development.
Water is another area where our
interests meet.
Drought can destroy crops,
threaten food and energy supplies,
and take away people's income.
Climate change is making these pressure
greater.
Rivers also cross borders.
What one country does can affect the
water available to another to another.
This makes cooperation essential.
Hungary has experience in water
management, sustainable agriculture, and
climate adaptation,
and we are ready to share it.
For many countries represented in this
hall, food, energy, education, health,
and jobs are immediate concern.
We must give these issues to the same
serious attention that we ask others to
give European security.
International cooperation works best
when it responds to people's real needs,
and when every country has a voice.
Excellencies,
the United Nations faces a crisis of
trust.
Too often, it fails to act when powerful
states and their friends break the law
rules. No country should be above the
law.
We cannot have one rule for our friends
and another for others.
But the answer is not to turn away from
the United Nations. We need it, and we
need it to work.
It must be able to act, treat all its
members fairly, and apply the same
principles to everyone.
Hungary is ready to do its part. We will
stand for human rights, support
peacekeeping, and work with countries
across the world to protect people and
help diplomacy succeed.
We must also look beyond the problems
today.
Many of the of the decisions we make now
will shape the the lives of people who
are not yet born.
A school, a strong institution, or a
safe water system can benefit people for
many years.
Future generations must therefore have a
place in the decisions we make today.
Hungary supports stronger international
action to protect their interest,
including the appointment of a United
Nations special envoy for future
generations.
The United Nations cannot demand trust.
It must earn it.
The same is true of every state and
every public institution.
The Hungarian people have asked us to
restore their confidence in the future.
We will honor that choice by rebuilding
trust at home and by becoming a country
others can trust when their own future
is at stake.
For Hungary, this is a new beginning.
But the principle behind is not new.
Power earns trust only when it accepts
law.
That is the responsibility that Hungary
accepts and the work we are ready to
undertake with you.
Thank you very much for your attention.
>> [applause]
>> On behalf of the assembly, I wish to
thank the president of Hungary.
